thread.title: Qualcomm will gain more than its rivals do, as artificial intelligence grows at the ‘edge’ - MarketWatch

author: Ryan Shrout
title: Qualcomm will gain more than its rivals do, as artificial intelligence grows at the ‘edge’ - MarketWatch
text:
The artificial intelligence market, though still in its infancy, is expected to be the primary driver for many technology companies in the next decade.
And it’s already going through some changes.
Shifts in how artificial intelligence (AI) is applied to computing and how consumers will interact with it are moving the emphasis from the server room to the devices in our pockets, a change that could benefit mobile-first players like Qualcomm QCOM, +1.49%
Data centers and edge are vital for AI In the current vision of AI, computing is associated with the cloud, large clusters of servers computing constantly in data centers. This model is led by Nvidia NVDA, +0.64% a company that CEO Jensen Huang has deftly maneuvered into the pole position for large-scale machine learning.
There are fast followers to watch, though, including both Intel INTC, +1.26% a stalwart in the data-center space, and Google GOOG, -0.33% building its own chips for AI processing. This need for server-based artificial intelligence won’t be going away as it is responsible for training the complex models and data sets required for AI to be applied on consumer and commercial devices. Training crunches down the complexity of artificial learning models into more compact tasks that can be addressed by client devices with much less horsepower.
But to scale to the trillions of connected devices expected to come online in the 2020s in which every facet of nearly all markets will be touched by AI, the intelligence computing required will need to be distributed to the edge. The “edge computing” segment covers where end user devices are, including laptops, smartphones, TVs, etc., and represents localized processing capability.
Qualcomm may not build phones or TVs itself, but it does build chips that go into everything from smartphones to watches to routers. This gives the San Diego-based company an opportunity to bring its flavor of AI processing to countless markets swiftly and with less friction from device manufacturers.
Other articles may mention the AI processing capability that other mobile chip companies offer, including those from Apple AAPL, +0.23% Samsung SSNLF, -3.07% and Hi-Silicon (the chip design portion of Chinese giant Huawei). While they do offer competitive AI performance with Qualcomm, Apple and Hi-Silicon design chips only for their own product verticals. Apple isn’t going to sell an A11 Bionic processor (used in the iPhone X) to someone for installation in a smart security camera or drone.
As a result, Qualcomm combines a technological advantage and a market advantage that no one else can duplicate in today’s environment.
Wireless advantage for Qualcomm Though the smartphone dominates headlines, analysts that believe the winner of the AI chip race in that market automatically means dominance in the greater AI landscape are missing the forest for the trees. The smartphone market is an important step in the progression, but the trillion-device opportunity expands well behind the screens in our pocket.
Qualcomm also has the ability to utilize its advantage in 5G wireless technology to help cement its spot with AI processor integration. With its lead in 5G time to market and intellectual property licensing, Qualcomm is already working with the leaders in automation, production, automobiles and security to build a new wave of interconnected devices and architectures. It will be an easy sell for Qualcomm to then provide complementary AI chips and processing to customers as the next step of innovation.
Yes, the first market ripe for AI integration at the edge will be the smartphone, and with more than 8.6 billion cumulative sales expected between 2018 and 2022, it will be a sizeable market with many competitors. Qualcomm is the leader in AP (application processor) sales in the Android space but expect to see competition from Apple and Samsung as the most interesting. But for Qualcomm, selling AI performance in smartphones is only the first step of a much larger plan of artificial-intelligence integration across the technology landscape.
Qualcomm has AI in its DNA For years Qualcomm has been talking to technical media and partners about machine learning and the advantages that its hardware platform provided. Early on in the discussion, the company leaned on the idea of “heterogeneous compute,” a complex idea of combining the capability of multiple processors built for general compute, graphics and digital-signal processing to provide the best balance of resources to the problems of machine learning.
That combination of different processing technology gives Qualcomm performance advantages and flexibility to adapt as the machine-learning landscape evolves, which it does frequently. Qualcomm is now calling this combo the “Snapdragon AI Engine,” a retroactive brand going back several generations of hardware.
While other vendors are developing dedicated AI processors called NPUs (neural processing units), Qualcomm still believes in the benefits of the AI Engine with varying components, all with strengths in key areas. Once AI computing models settle to some semblance of a standard, I would expect Qualcomm to venture down that same path, however, creating a specific set of IP for AI and machine-learning applications.
Experience in mobile technology Mapping the challenges of AI workloads to a mobile-focused chip at the edge is a unique problem. While you have virtually unlimited power and space in the data center to address machine learning, in a smartphone or drone or security camera you are restrained by thermal and battery limits. Qualcomm has decades of experience doing this, bringing as much compute performance as possible into a small, efficient piece of silicon that sip power while meeting performance requirements.
Qualcomm already did this for the virtual reality (VR) space. Even when high-performance virtual reality was powered by dedicated, expensive PCs and tethered headsets, Snapdragon VR reference designs brought efficiency and performance to the forefront in order to offer VR experiences to a mobile platform and design. This tends to help lower prices for mass-market adoption, as we saw with the recent Oculus Go launch from Facebook FB, -0.54%
Part of the company’s AI Engine platform revolves around helping developers address performance and power concerns with software tools for model compression, the act of minimizing the memory and storage required for effective AI use. Qualcomm claims that over the past 12 months alone, it has created a 200% increase in AI performance for its platforms, a fact that it hopes showcases its capability for the coming wave of AI-enabled internet of things.
Ryan Shrout is the founder and lead analyst at Shrout Research , and the owner of PC Perspective . Follow him on Twitter @ryanshrout .
Ryan Shrout Ryan Shrout is the founder and lead analyst at Shrout Research, consulting and advising leaders in the mobile, graphics, processors and platforms industry. He has 17 years of experience evaluating and analyzing hardware and technology as the owner of PC Perspective. Shrout has worked with technology giants and their product-management teams, including Intel, Qualcomm, AMD, Nvidia and Microsoft.
